summary: A second version of a proposed mail box protocol, designed as a subset of the File Transfer Protocol. Each site would have a write-only sequential file to which messages and documents sent over the network are appended, to be printed or used later. This was an early step toward network mail. It was replaced by RFC 278.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 221 proposes a standard way to add a message or document to a mail-box file at another site. The design uses a file-transfer request and printer-oriented defaults, and it was later replaced by RFC 278.

questions: what was the mail box protocol
how did the mail box protocol append messages
subtitle: A proposal for appending network messages to a site's mail box

tldr.problem: The NIC needed to send documents to remote sites without knowing their file-system naming rules, and to receive documents from them.
tldr.mechanism: A sender requests an append to a numbered mail box, sends the file using File Transfer Protocol conventions, and receives an acknowledgment.
tldr.outcome: RFC 221 was an early mail-box proposal and was later replaced by RFC 278.

sections.title: A Standard Mail Box
sections.content:
The Mail Box Protocol gives each site a standard way to receive sequential files for immediate or later printing, or for other uses. A mail box is a network-write-only sequential file to which messages and documents are appended.

The proposal addresses the NIC's need to deliver documents without knowing each site's path-name conventions, and to receive documents for cataloging or redistribution. It allows 256 mail boxes at a site; mail box 0 is the default for the standard printer.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail box is a file at a remote site where a sender can add a document. The protocol gives senders a shared name for the destination without requiring them to know the site's file paths.

sections.title: The Standard Printer Format
sections.content:
Mail box 0 defaults to Network ASCII and assumes a printer with lines 72 characters wide and pages of 66 lines. A new line uses carriage return followed by line feed, and form feed moves to the top of a new page.

The sender controls line and page lengths. The beginning of a message for mail box 0 contains an address string with sender and receiver details, ending with a form feed. The protocol does not define the contents of other mail boxes.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail box 0 is formatted for a printer, so a message starts with sender and receiver details and uses printer line and page controls. Other mail boxes can have formats that this RFC does not define.

sections.title: Appending a Mail Item
sections.content:
The protocol uses established network procedures and File Transfer Protocol conventions. Its basic operation is append: the sender makes an append request, transfers the mail item in one or more data transactions, indicates end of file, and receives an acknowledgment.

Control transactions identify a data type, report an error, acknowledge success, request an append, or change printer settings. The RFC notes a concern that senders could flood a site's printer with unwanted data; it recommends that initial implementations use site-dependent safeguards rather than defining standard protections.
sections.plainLanguage: To deliver a document, the sender requests permission to append it, sends the data, marks the end, and waits for acknowledgment. The RFC leaves safeguards against unwanted volume to each site.
